lead: Scan design makes a sequential chip testable by turning its flip-flops into one or more long shift registers during test. In normal mode each flip-flop takes its functional input. In scan mode the same flip-flops are chained, so the tester can shift any pattern into every state bit, run one functional clock, and shift the captured result out. The hard sequential problem becomes an easy combinational one. Full scan is standard in digital ASICs and SoCs; some syllabi call it scan-path design or scan-based DFT.
prereq: You need: the D flip-flop and the 2:1 multiplexer, from the chapter on latches and registers, and combinational ATPG from 6.3.

sections.h3: Why sequential circuits are hard, and ad hoc DFT

blocks.text: A combinational circuit is easy to test: apply a vector at the pins, wait, compare the outputs. A sequential circuit hides its state. To set one internal flip-flop to 1, the tester may need a long sequence of clocked input vectors, and the effect of a fault must then travel through more state to reach a pin. Controllability is how easily a node can be set to 0 or 1 from the primary inputs; observability is how easily its value can be seen at a primary output. Both get worse as the state grows, and ATPG time explodes.
Design for testability (DFT) means adding hardware or following rules so the chip is cheap to test. Ad hoc DFT is a set of good habits, applied case by case:

items: add test points: a control point (a gate or multiplexer that forces a node) and an observation point (a node brought to a pin or a register);
partition a large block so each part can be tested on its own;
give every flip-flop a reset, so the state starts known;
avoid asynchronous logic and combinational feedback loops, or break them in test mode;
split long counters, and let the tester bypass on-chip oscillators and clock dividers.

blocks.text: These help, but they give no systematic method. Structured DFT, scan and BIST, changes the design so every state bit can be loaded and read.

sections.h3: Muxed-D scan cell, full scan and partial scan

blocks.text: The standard muxed-D scan cell puts a 2:1 multiplexer in front of a D flip-flop. Its inputs are the functional data D and the scan input SI; the select is scan enable SE. With SE = 0 the cell is a normal flip-flop; with SE = 1 it takes SI. Joining Q of one cell to SI of the next makes a shift register, the scan chain, from the chip's scan-in pin to its scan-out pin.

Full scan makes every flip-flop a scan cell. ATPG then treats each flip-flop output as a pseudo-primary input and each flip-flop input as a pseudo-primary output, and sees only the combinational logic between them. Partial scan converts only some flip-flops, usually those that break feedback loops; it saves area and delay but leaves a small sequential circuit for ATPG.

The costs: a multiplexer and extra wiring per flip-flop (a few per cent of logic area), one multiplexer delay on every functional D path, an SE net that reaches every cell, and two or more extra pins. During shift, if clock skew between two neighbouring cells is large, the later cell can catch the new value its neighbour has just launched instead of the old one, a hold-time race; a lock-up latch between cells on different clocks prevents it. LSSD, level-sensitive scan design, reaches the same goal with latches and two non-overlapping clocks instead of a multiplexer.

sections.h3: The scan test procedure and its cost

items: Shift in: SE = 1; the pattern is clocked into the chain one bit per clock. The bit meant for the last cell goes in first.
Capture: SE = 0; one functional clock loads the combinational logic's response into the flip-flops. Primary outputs are compared at the same time.
Shift out: SE = 1; the captured bits leave through scan-out and the tester compares each with its expected value. The next pattern shifts in during the same clocks.

blocks.where: where N is the length of the longest chain, P the number of patterns, the 1 is the capture clock, and the last N is the final shift-out. Test time = cycles × scan clock period.

blocks.text: Splitting the flip-flops into K balanced chains cuts N to about N ÷ K, so test time falls almost K times, but each chain needs its own scan-in and scan-out pin. Scan makes ATPG easy and can reduce the number of patterns, yet every pattern still costs N shift clocks.

spec.aria: Three multiplexer and flip-flop scan cells in a chain from SI to SO, below a logic block that computes D1, D2 and D3 from Q1, Q2 and Q3, with the pattern and the captured values.

examples.question: A chip has three scan cells chained SI → FF1 → FF2 → FF3 → SO. The logic feeding them is D1 = Q2·Q3, D2 = Q1 ⊕ Q3 and D3 = NOT Q1. Load the pattern Q1Q2Q3 = 011 to test the AND output D1 stuck-at-0, capture, and shift out. Give the bits on SO for the good and the faulty chip.
steps: To leave FF3 = 1, FF2 = 1, FF1 = 0 after three shifts, apply SI = 1, 1, 0 in that order (the bit for FF3 first).
Capture with SE = 0: good D1 = 1·1 = 1, D2 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1, D3 = NOT 0 = 1, so the cells hold 111. With D1 stuck-at-0, FF1 captures 0 and the cells hold 011.
Shift out: SO shows Q3, then Q2, then Q1. Good: 1, 1, 1. Faulty: 1, 1, 0. The third bit out differs, so the fault is detected.
Count: 3 shift-in + 1 capture + 3 shift-out = 7 clocks = (N + 1)P + N with N = 3, P = 1.
examples.answer: The pattern 011 shifted in as SI = 1, 1, 0 gives SO = 1, 1, 1 on a good chip and 1, 1, 0 on a chip with D1 stuck-at-0; the third bit out shows the fault.

examples.question: A design has 200 flip-flops in one scan chain and needs 1000 scan patterns. The scan clock is 100 MHz. Find the total test time. Then split the flip-flops into 4 balanced chains of 50 and find it again.
steps: Per pattern: 201 cycles = 2.01 µs, of which 2.00 µs is shifting.
examples.answer: 2.012 ms with one chain and 0.511 ms with four chains, 3.94 times faster, at the price of three more scan-in and three more scan-out pins.

traps: Forgetting the final shift-out. P patterns cost (N + 1)P + N clocks, not (N + 1)P; the last response still has to leave the chain.
Shifting the pattern in the wrong order. The first bit in ends in the cell farthest from scan-in.
SE polarity: here SE = 1 shifts and SE = 0 captures. Read the definition the question gives.
Saying scan has no delay cost. The multiplexer sits on every functional D path.
Calling LSSD a muxed-D design. LSSD uses latches with two non-overlapping clocks and no multiplexer.

quiz.q: What does SE = 1 select in a muxed-D scan cell?
quiz.a: The scan input SI, so the cell shifts the bit from the previous cell.

quiz.q: Name the three phases of a scan test.
quiz.a: Shift in, capture, shift out (the shift-out of one pattern overlaps the shift-in of the next).

quiz.q: Why does full scan make ATPG easier for a sequential circuit?
quiz.a: Every state bit can be set and read directly through the chain, so ATPG treats flip-flops as pseudo-primary inputs and outputs and works on combinational logic only.

quiz.q: Give two ad hoc DFT rules and say what each fixes.
quiz.a: A reset on every flip-flop gives a known starting state (controllability). A test point that brings a buried node to a pin or register lets the tester see it (observability).

quiz.q: A chain has 300 flip-flops, the scan clock is 50 MHz and there are 500 patterns. Find the total test time.
In the first worked example, which pattern would you load to test D3 stuck-at-1, and what does SO show for the good chip?
quiz.a: D3 = NOT Q1, so set Q1 = 1 to make the good D3 = 0. Take Q1Q2Q3 = 100: capture gives D1 = 0·0 = 0, D2 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1, D3 = 0, cells 010. SO shows Q3, Q2, Q1 = 0, 1, 0 for the good chip; the faulty chip shows 1, 1, 0.

quiz.q: A scan chain passes simulation but corrupts data during shift on silicon. Give a likely cause and a fix.
quiz.a: A hold-time race from clock skew: a cell catches the value its neighbour launched on the same edge. Fix it with a lock-up latch between cells on different clock branches, or by balancing the clock tree.

beyond: Not for the exam. Large chips compress scan data: a small decompressor feeds hundreds of short internal chains from a few tester pins, and a compactor squeezes their outputs (see 6.8). At-speed scan launches delay tests either from the last shift (launch-on-shift) or from a first capture (launch-on-capture). Search 'scan compression', 'launch-on-capture' and 'lock-up latch'.
